decks.title: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm — Part 1: Meaning, Modes, Section 48 and the Realisation Account
goals: Distinguish dissolution of partnership from dissolution of the firm
Identify the five modes of dissolution under the Indian Partnership Act 1932
Apply the Section 48 order of settlement
Explain what the Realisation Account records and what stays out of it

slides.heading: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **partnership or firm?**, the **modes** of dissolution, the **Section 48** order and the **Realisation Account**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: dissolution of partnership versus dissolution of the firm, the five modes of dissolution, the order of settlement under Section 48, and the Realisation Account
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every firm eventually changes or closes. In this chapter we study the day a firm closes for good. First we separate two ideas that sound alike: dissolving a partnership and dissolving a firm. Then we see the five ways a firm can be dissolved, the legal order in which its money is paid out, and the special account that records the closing: the Realisation Account.

slides.heading: Partnership or firm: what is dissolved?
columns:
**Dissolution of partnership**

- The old agreement ends.
- The business carries on.
- Books continue.

**Dissolution of the firm**

- The business is closed.
- Assets are sold, liabilities paid.
- Books are closed.

rows: The old agreement among the partners
The business and every partner’s relationship
Admission, retirement, death, change in ratio
Agreement to close, unlawful business, court order

visual.alt: Table comparing dissolution of partnership, where only the agreement ends and the business and books carry on, with dissolution of the firm, where the business is closed, assets are sold, liabilities paid and the books closed

slides.narration: When a partner joins, retires or dies, or the partners change their ratio, the old agreement ends and a new one begins. That is dissolution of partnership, and the firm carries on. Dissolution of the firm is final: the business stops, the assets are sold, the debts are paid, the partners are settled and the books are closed.

slides.heading: Two different paths

nodes.label: Partnership dissolved; the firm carries on
Firm dissolved; the partnership ends too

visual.alt: Two paths: a change among the partners, such as a retirement, dissolves only the partnership and the firm carries on; closing the business dissolves the firm, and with it the partnership
visual.caption: Every dissolution of a firm is also a dissolution of partnership; not the other way round

slides.narration: Picture two separate paths. A change among the partners leads only to a new partnership, and the same firm goes on trading. Closing the business leads to dissolution of the firm, and since every partner’s relationship then ends, the partnership is dissolved as well. So dissolving a firm always dissolves the partnership, but not the other way round.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: partnership only, or the firm?
slides.body_md: Decide for each imagined situation.

rows: Kiran retires; Lina and Manoj carry on the shop
Three partners change their ratio from 3:2:1 to 1:1:1
All the partners agree to close the shop and sell its stock
A new partner is admitted for a 1/5 share

visual.alt: Table of four situations: a retirement, a change of ratio and an admission dissolve only the partnership; an agreement to close the shop dissolves the firm as well

slides.narration: Look at each case and ask one question: does the business go on? When Kiran retires and the others continue, it does, so only the partnership is dissolved. The same is true of a change in ratio and of admitting a new partner. But when all the partners agree to close the shop and sell its stock, the business ends, so the firm itself is dissolved.

slides.heading: Quick check: partnership or firm?
slides.body_md: Which event leaves the firm alive?
slides.narration: Look for the one event after which the same business keeps trading.

slides.heading: The five modes of dissolution

rows: All partners consent, or as the contract provides
By law, e.g. the business becomes unlawful
Fixed term ends, venture completed, death of a partner (unless agreed otherwise)
Partnership at will: written notice by any partner
On a partner’s suit, on grounds the Act lists

visual.alt: Table of the five modes of dissolution under the Indian Partnership Act: by agreement, compulsory, on the happening of contingencies, by notice in a partnership at will, and by the court on a partner’s suit
visual.caption: Indian Partnership Act 1932, Sections 40–44

slides.narration: The Indian Partnership Act gives five ways in which a firm may be dissolved. The partners may simply agree. The law may force it. Certain events may end it, unless the partners have agreed otherwise. In a partnership at will, any partner may end it by notice. And finally, a court may order it when a partner files a suit.

slides.heading: Compulsory dissolution and contingencies
columns:
**Compulsory**

- By law.
- The partners’ wishes do not matter.

**Contingencies**

- Term over, venture done, a partner dies.
- Unless agreed otherwise.

rows: Happens by law, even if the partners want to continue
Happens unless the partners have agreed otherwise
Example: a new law bans the firm’s trade
The fixed term of the firm ends
Example: the business can no longer be carried on lawfully
The venture the firm was formed for is completed

visual.alt: Table: compulsory dissolution happens by law, for example when the firm’s trade is banned; dissolution on contingencies happens, unless agreed otherwise, when a fixed term ends, a venture is completed or a partner dies

slides.narration: Compulsory dissolution happens by force of law. If a new law bans the trade a firm carries on, the firm ends at once, whatever the partners want. Contingencies are different: the firm ends when its fixed term runs out, when the venture it was formed for is complete, or when a partner dies, but only if the partners have not agreed to carry on.

slides.heading: Dissolution by notice and by the court
bullets: **By notice:** only in a partnership at will; written notice to all the other partners.
**By the court:** only when a partner files a suit and a ground in the Act applies.

headers: Ground for dissolution by the court (Section 44)
rows: A partner loses mental capacity; another partner sues
A partner can never again do his share of the work
A partner keeps signing contracts the deed forbids
A partner sells his entire share to an outsider
Losses every year with no hope of recovery
Deadlock: the partners cannot work together at all

visual.alt: Table of grounds on which the court may dissolve a firm on a partner’s suit: unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct or persistent breach, transfer of a partner’s whole interest, a business run only at a loss, and any just and equitable ground
visual.caption: Dissolution by notice (Section 43) needs a partnership at will and a written notice.

slides.narration: In a partnership at will, any partner can end the firm by giving written notice to all the others. A court, on the other hand, acts only when a partner files a suit. The Act lists grounds such as a partner of unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of the agreement, transfer of a whole share, a business that can run only at a loss, or any just and equitable reason.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the modes
slides.body_md: Match each situation with its mode.
slides.narration: For each situation, ask what ended the firm: consent, the law, a written notice, or a court order.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming the mode
slides.body_md: Name the mode and the section for each imagined firm.

rows: A firm formed to run one trade fair; the fair is over
A partner in a firm at will writes to the others ending it from 1 July
The partners all sign a resolution to close the firm
A partner sells his whole share to an outsider; another partner sues

visual.alt: Table naming the mode for four situations: a completed venture is a contingency, a written notice in a firm at will is dissolution by notice, a resolution of all partners is dissolution by agreement, and a transfer of a whole interest followed by a suit is dissolution by the court

slides.narration: A firm formed only for one trade fair ends when the fair is over: a contingency, section forty-two. A written notice in a firm at will is dissolution by notice, section forty-three. A resolution signed by every partner is dissolution by agreement, section forty. And a partner who sells his whole share to an outsider gives the others a ground to go to court, section forty-four.

slides.heading: Settlement of accounts: Section 48

nodes.label: Losses: out of profits, then capital, then partners personally (profit-sharing ratio)

visual.alt: Flow of Section 48: losses are met out of profits, then capital, then by partners personally; the assets then pay outside debts first, partners’ loans second, partners’ capitals third, and any surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio
visual.caption: Section 48, Indian Partnership Act 1932 (unless the partners agree otherwise)

slides.narration: Once the firm is dissolved, who gets paid first? Section forty-eight answers this, unless the partners have agreed otherwise. Losses are met from profits, then from capital, and if needed by the partners personally. The assets then pay outsiders first, partners’ loans next, partners’ capitals after that, and any surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined bakery in Shimla owned by Meena and Nitin. After every asset is sold, the bank holds rupees two lakh ten thousand. The creditors take rupees ninety thousand first. Meena's loan of rupees forty thousand comes next. Only what is left goes to the capitals, after the loss has been charged to them.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: Section 48 at an imagined bakery
slides.body_md: Creditors ₹90,000; Meena's loan ₹40,000; capitals Meena ₹50,000 and Nitin ₹40,000; partners share equally; bank after realisation ₹2,10,000.

visual.alt: Table of worked example: claims total 2,20,000 against 2,10,000 available, a loss of 10,000 shared equally; creditors and Meena's loan are paid in full and the capitals are paid 45,000 and 35,000
visual.caption: Loss = 2,20,000 − 2,10,000 = 10,000.

slides.narration: The claims add up to rupees two lakh twenty thousand, but only rupees two lakh ten thousand is available, so the loss is rupees ten thousand. It is shared equally and taken out of the capitals. Creditors and the loan are paid in full, then Meena receives rupees forty-five thousand and Nitin rupees thirty-five thousand. Every rupee in the bank is used up.

slides.heading: The Realisation Account

rows: All assets except cash, bank and fictitious assets, at book value (debtors gross)
Cash paid to settle outside liabilities
All outside liabilities at book value
Realisation expenses borne by the firm
Cash received from assets, including unrecorded ones
Liabilities or expenses taken over or paid by a partner
Assets taken over by partners at agreed values

visual.alt: Format of the Realisation Account: on the debit side, assets at book value, cash paid for liabilities, realisation expenses, items paid or taken over by partners, and any profit; on the credit side, provisions, outside liabilities, cash from assets, assets taken over by partners, and any loss

slides.narration: To close the books we open a Realisation Account. It is a nominal account. Assets other than cash and bank are moved to its debit side at book value, and outside liabilities to its credit side. As assets are sold and liabilities paid, the money is recorded against it. Its balance is the profit or loss on realisation, shared by the partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

slides.heading: What stays out of the Realisation Account

rows: Paid from the bank, after outside liabilities
Capital accounts, closed at the end
General Reserve; Profit and Loss credit balance
Profit and Loss debit balance; deferred revenue expenditure

visual.alt: Table of items that do not pass through the Realisation Account: cash and bank, partners’ loans, capitals and current accounts, reserves and accumulated profits, and accumulated losses or deferred revenue expenditure

slides.narration: Not everything goes into the Realisation Account. Cash and bank are already money, so they stay in the Cash or Bank Account. A partner’s loan is paid directly from the bank. Reserves and accumulated profits go straight to the capitals, and so do accumulated losses and deferred expenses, in the profit-sharing ratio.

slides.heading: Meet Narmada Textiles
slides.body_md: An imagined firm in Jabalpur. **Asha, Bhavesh and Charu** share profits **3:2:1** and dissolve the firm on 31 March 2026. We follow it to the end of Part 2.

rows: Debtors 50,000 less Provision for Doubtful Debts 2,000

visual.caption: Asha, Bhavesh and Charu share profits 3:2:1.

slides.narration: Narmada Textiles is our running example. Its balance sheet shows creditors, bills payable, a loan from Bhavesh, a general reserve and the three capitals. On the assets side are building, machinery, furniture, stock, debtors with a small provision against them, and rupees twenty-six thousand at the bank. Both sides total rupees three lakh seventy-four thousand.

slides.body_md: The first two entries on dissolution move the assets and outside liabilities to the Realisation Account.
bullets: Debtors go at the **gross** figure; the provision is credited separately.
Bank, Bhavesh’s loan, the reserve and the capitals are **not** transferred.

rows: *(Being assets transferred to the Realisation Account)*
Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c Dr
*(Being provision and outside liabilities transferred to the Realisation Account)*

visual.alt: Journal entries for Narmada Textiles: Realisation debited 3,50,000 for building, machinery, furniture, stock and debtors; provision, creditors and bills payable debited and Realisation credited 82,000

slides.narration: Realisation is debited with rupees three lakh fifty thousand, the book value of the five assets, with debtors at their full amount. Then the provision, the creditors and the bills payable are debited and Realisation is credited with rupees eighty-two thousand. The bank balance, the loan, the reserve and the capitals stay where they are.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Firm dissolved = business closed; partnership dissolved = agreement changed
Nominal account: assets (Dr) and outside liabilities (Cr) at book value
Cash/bank, partners’ loans, capitals, reserves, accumulated losses

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the difference between dissolving the partnership and the firm, the five modes with their sections, the Section 48 order of payment, the Realisation Account, and the items kept out of it

slides.narration: To sum up: dissolving a firm closes the business, while dissolving a partnership only changes the agreement. A firm may be dissolved by agreement, compulsorily, on contingencies, by notice or by the court. Section forty-eight pays outsiders first, then partners’ loans, then capitals. And the Realisation Account collects the assets and outside liabilities so that the result of closing can be found.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: When asked to distinguish, give **three clear bases** in a table.
Name the **section** with each mode: agreement 40, compulsory 41, contingencies 42, notice 43, court 44.
Transfer **debtors gross** and credit the **provision** separately.
Never transfer **cash, bank, partners’ loans, capitals or reserves** to Realisation.
slides.narration: A few tips for the board exam. Present distinctions in a table with at least three bases. Mention the section of the Act with each mode. Learn the Section forty-eight order as a chain: outsiders, loans, capitals, surplus. And when you open the Realisation Account, transfer debtors at their full figure and keep cash, loans, capitals and reserves out of it.

goals: Record the sale of assets and the payment of liabilities
Record assets and liabilities taken over by partners, and unrecorded items
Treat realisation expenses and a partner’s remuneration correctly
Prepare the Realisation Account, partners’ capital and loan accounts and a Bank Account that closes at nil

slides.heading: Closing the books of a dissolved firm
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **realising assets**, **paying liabilities**, **takeovers**, **unrecorded items**, **expenses**, and the final **capital** and **Bank** accounts.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: selling assets and paying liabilities, takeovers by partners, unrecorded items, realisation expenses, partners’ capital and loan accounts, and the Bank Account closing at nil
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we opened the Realisation Account. Now we fill it. We sell assets, pay liabilities and record what partners take over. We deal with items that were never in the books and with the costs of closing. Then we settle each partner and watch the Bank Account close at exactly nil.

slides.heading: Selling assets and paying liabilities

rows: Bank A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c
Outside liability paid (full or at a discount)
Realisation A/c Dr, To Bank A/c (amount actually paid)
No entry (its book value stays on the debit side)

visual.alt: Table of entries: an asset sold for cash is Bank debit, Realisation credit; a liability paid is Realisation debit, Bank credit for the amount actually paid; a worthless asset needs no entry

slides.narration: When an asset is sold, the cash comes into the bank and the Realisation Account is credited. When a liability is paid, Realisation is debited with the amount actually paid, which may be less than the book figure if the creditor allows a discount. An asset that fetches nothing needs no entry: its book value simply stays on the debit side as a loss.

slides.heading: Partners who take over assets or liabilities

rows: Partner’s Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c
Gets less cash at the end
Realisation A/c Dr, To Partner’s Capital A/c
Gets more cash at the end
Partner pays expenses for the firm
Realisation A/c Dr, To Partner’s Capital A/c
Gets more cash at the end

visual.alt: Table of partner transactions: taking over an asset debits the partner’s capital and credits Realisation; taking over a liability or paying firm expenses debits Realisation and credits the partner’s capital

slides.narration: Partners often take assets home instead of cash. Then the partner’s capital is debited and Realisation is credited with the agreed value. If a partner agrees to pay a liability, or pays an expense for the firm, the opposite happens: Realisation is debited and the partner’s capital is credited, because the firm now owes him more.

slides.body_md: Narmada Textiles (from Part 1) on dissolution:

visual.alt: Table of the events on dissolution of Narmada Textiles: building, machinery, debtors and an unrecorded computer realise cash; Asha takes the furniture and Charu the stock; creditors, bills payable and expenses are paid

slides.narration: At Narmada Textiles the building fetches rupees one lakh thirty-four thousand, machinery rupees ninety-two thousand, debtors rupees forty-six thousand, and an old computer that was never recorded fetches rupees five thousand. Asha takes the furniture and Charu the stock. Creditors accept rupees fifty-eight thousand in full settlement, bills payable are paid in full and expenses come to rupees four thousand.

slides.body_md: Every event goes to one side of the Realisation Account.

rows: By Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c
By Asha's Capital A/c (Furniture taken over)
By Charu's Capital A/c (Stock taken over)

visual.alt: Realisation Account of Narmada Textiles: assets of 3,50,000 and payments of 82,000 on the debit side; provision, liabilities, cash from assets and takeovers on the credit side; profit 18,000 shared 9,000, 6,000 and 3,000
visual.caption: Profit on realisation ₹18,000, shared 3:2:1.

slides.narration: Debit the five assets and every payment. Credit the provision, the two liabilities, the cash from assets and the two takeovers. The credit side is larger by rupees eighteen thousand, a profit on realisation. Shared three to two to one, Asha gets rupees nine thousand, Bhavesh rupees six thousand and Charu rupees three thousand.

slides.narration: To sum up: assets sold and assets taken over are credited to Realisation; liabilities paid or taken over and firm expenses are debited to it. A creditor who accepts an asset in full needs no entry. The realisation result, reserves and losses go to the capitals. Loans are repaid before capitals, debit balances are made good in cash, and the Bank Account closes at nil.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Prepare **Realisation → Capitals → Bank**, in that order.
Record only the **cash actually paid** to creditors; no entry for an asset handed over in full settlement.
Expenses a **partner must bear** never go to Realisation.
Settle a partner’s **debit balance** before paying the others.
Your Bank Account **must close at nil**: if it does not, look for a missed item.
slides.narration: Some final advice. Prepare the Realisation Account first, then the capital accounts, then the Bank Account. Record only cash that actually moves. Keep expenses that a partner must bear out of Realisation. Bring in cash for any debit balance before paying the others. And always check that your Bank Account closes at nil; it is your built-in test.

sections.heading: 1. Dissolution of partnership and dissolution of the firm
sections.body_md:
**Dissolution of partnership:** the existing agreement among the partners ends, for example on admission, retirement or death of a partner or a change in the profit-sharing ratio. The firm is **reconstituted** and its business and books carry on.

**Dissolution of the firm:** the business is closed and the relationship among **all** partners ends. Assets are realised, liabilities paid, partners settled and the books closed.

Dissolution of a firm always includes dissolution of the partnership; a dissolution of partnership need not end the firm.

sections.heading: 3. Settlement of accounts: Section 48
sections.body_md:
Unless the partners have agreed otherwise:

**Losses** (including a deficiency of capital) are borne in this order: from profits → from capital → by the partners personally in their profit-sharing ratio.

**The firm’s assets** (with any cash the partners bring in) are applied in this order:
1. Outside liabilities (debts to third parties).
2. Partners’ loans (advances), rateably.
3. Partners’ capitals, rateably.
4. Any residue, in the profit-sharing ratio.

**Worked figure (imagined bakery):** claims 2,20,000 − cash 2,10,000 = loss 10,000; capitals fall to 45,000 and 35,000.

sections.heading: 4. The Realisation Account: transfers

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Transferring **cash, bank, a partner’s loan or reserves** to the Realisation Account.
- Transferring debtors at the net figure **and** crediting the provision (counting it twice).
- Recording an entry when a creditor accepts an asset in **full settlement**.
- Debiting Realisation with expenses that a **partner must bear**.
- Paying capitals before **partners’ loans**, or paying a partner before another partner’s **debit balance** is made good.
- A Bank Account that does not close at nil: an item has been missed.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: correct option or entry.
- 3 marks: three journal entries, or a distinction on three bases.
- 4 marks: a Realisation Account, or a set of four entries with step marks.
- 6 marks: Realisation Account (about 2–3) + capital accounts (about 2) + Bank Account (about 1), or a full set of journal entries.

**Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:** piecemeal distribution of cash, sale of a firm to a company, and insolvency of partners (including its accounting treatment) are excluded from this chapter and are not examined.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

Dissolution **by the court** on a partner’s suit.
Unsound mind or permanent incapacity of a partner; persistent breach of agreement; business only at a loss (any two).
**Outsiders → partners’ loans → capitals → surplus** (profit-sharing ratio).
From profits, then capital, then partners personally in the profit-sharing ratio.
A **nominal** account that finds the profit or loss on closing the firm.

Not in Realisation; **Loan A/c Dr, To Bank A/c**, after outsiders, before capitals.
Credited to capitals in the **profit-sharing ratio**.
Debited to capitals in the **profit-sharing ratio**.

cards.back_md: **Partner’s Capital A/c Dr**, To Realisation A/c.

questions.stem_md: Dissolution of a partnership firm means that

options.text_md: one partner leaves and the remaining partners carry on the business
the business of the firm is closed and the relationship among all the partners comes to an end
a new partner joins and the profit-sharing ratio changes
the partners change their profit-sharing ratio and carry on the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the business of the firm is closed and the relationship among all the partners comes to an end. When the firm itself is dissolved, the business is wound up: assets are realised, liabilities are paid and the partners are settled. The other three are reconstitutions, in which only the partnership changes and the firm survives.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following results in the dissolution of the partnership but **not** in the dissolution of the firm?

options.text_md: The business of the firm becoming unlawful
All the partners agreeing to close the business
A court order winding up the firm on a partner’s suit
Retirement of a partner, the others carrying on the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Retirement of a partner, the others carrying on the business. On retirement the old agreement ends but the remaining partners continue the same business, so only the partnership is reconstituted. The other three end the business itself.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm in Kozhikode imports a herbal product. A new law bans all trade in that product. The firm will be dissolved

options.text_md: compulsorily, because its business has become unlawful
only if all the partners agree to it
only if the court orders it on a partner’s suit
only when the term of the partnership expires

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** compulsorily, because its business has become unlawful. Section 41 dissolves a firm automatically, whatever the partners want, when its business becomes illegal; no agreement, notice or court order is needed.

questions.stem_md: Shalini and Vikas formed an imagined firm in Madurai for a fixed period of three years to run a crafts kiosk. Nothing else is agreed. When the three years end, the firm is dissolved

options.text_md: by notice
compulsorily, because the business has become unlawful
on the happening of a contingency, the expiry of its fixed term
by the court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** on the happening of a contingency, the expiry of its fixed term. Section 42 lists events that dissolve a firm unless the partners agree otherwise: expiry of a fixed term, completion of the venture, and death of a partner, among others.

questions.stem_md: A partner can dissolve a firm simply by giving notice to the other partners only when

options.text_md: the partnership is for a fixed term
the partnership deed forbids dissolution
the partnership is at will
the court has already ordered dissolution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the partnership is at will. Section 43 allows dissolution by notice only in a partnership at will, that is, one with no fixed period or particular venture. The notice must be in writing to all the other partners.

questions.stem_md: On which of the following grounds may the court dissolve a firm when a partner files a suit?

options.text_md: A partner has become permanently incapable of performing his duties as a partner
All the partners have agreed to close the business
A new law has made the business of the firm unlawful
The partners wish to change their profit-sharing ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A partner has become permanently incapable of performing his duties as a partner. Permanent incapacity is one of the Section 44 grounds. Closing by consent is dissolution by agreement; an unlawful business is dissolved compulsorily without the court; a change of ratio is only a reconstitution.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dissolution of a firm always involves dissolution of the partnership.

**Reason (R):** When a firm is dissolved, its business is closed and the relationship among all the partners comes to an end.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Since every partner’s relationship ends when the firm closes, the partnership necessarily ends too; R explains A. The reverse is not true: a partnership can be dissolved while the firm continues.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The retirement of a partner always results in the dissolution of the firm.

**Reason (R):** On the retirement of a partner, the partnership among the partners is reconstituted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the continuing partners normally carry on the business, so the firm survives. R is true: the old agreement ends and a new one takes its place.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm is compulsorily dissolved when its business becomes unlawful.

**Reason (R):** A partner may ask the court to dissolve a firm when another partner becomes of unsound mind.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but they describe two different modes. R is a ground for dissolution by the court; it does not explain why an unlawful business ends the firm automatically.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A firm whose business becomes illegal can be dissolved only by an order of the court.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An unlawful business is a case of compulsory dissolution under Section 41: the firm ends by law without any court order.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a partnership at will, the notice of dissolution given by a partner must be in writing.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Section 43 requires written notice to all the other partners; the firm stands dissolved from the date mentioned in it or, if none, from the date of communication.

questions.stem_md: A partnership at will may be dissolved by any partner giving notice in ___ to all the other partners.
questions.solution_md: The notice must be given in writing.

questions.stem_md: Match each situation in column A with the mode of dissolution in column B.

options.text_md: The business of the firm becomes unlawful
All the partners consent to close the firm
A partner in a partnership at will writes to the others ending the firm
A partner becomes permanently incapable of working, and another partner sues

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Unlawful business: Section 41. Mutual consent: Section 40. Written notice in a partnership at will: Section 43. Permanent incapacity on a partner’s suit: Section 44.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between dissolution of partnership and dissolution of a partnership firm on any three bases.
questions.solution_md: Any three bases with both columns correct earn the marks.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Dissolution of partnership | Dissolution of the firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business | Continues under the reconstituted firm | Is closed |
| Relationship | Ends between the outgoing partner and the others; the rest continue | Ends among all the partners |
| Books of account | Are kept going; assets and liabilities are revalued | Are closed; assets are realised and liabilities paid |
| Role of the court | No court order is involved | The firm may be dissolved by the court |
| Link | Need not lead to dissolution of the firm | Always means dissolution of the partnership too |

questions.stem_md: State any three grounds on which the court may order the dissolution of a partnership firm on the suit of a partner.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each correct ground, up to three.

answer.model_answer_md:
Any three of the following (Section 44):

1. A partner has become of **unsound mind**.
2. A partner has become **permanently incapable** of performing his duties as a partner.
3. A partner is guilty of **misconduct** likely to harm the carrying on of the business.
4. A partner **wilfully or persistently breaches** the partnership agreement, or behaves so that the others cannot reasonably carry on the business with him.
5. A partner has **transferred his whole interest** in the firm to a third party.
6. The business **cannot be carried on except at a loss**.
7. Any other ground on which the court finds dissolution **just and equitable**.

questions.stem_md:
Identify, with reason, the mode of dissolution in each case:

(a) Nirmala, Joseph and Pritam formed an imagined firm in Panaji only to organise a single beach festival. The festival is over.
(b) Rafiq and Lalita run an imagined firm in Agra that trades in ivory carvings. A new law prohibits all trade in ivory.
(c) Kamal and Suraj have a partnership at will in an imagined shop in Ajmer. Kamal writes to Suraj that the firm will close from 1 June.
questions.solution_md: Look for the trigger in each case: the venture completed, the law changed, or a written notice in a partnership at will.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **On the happening of a contingency** (Section 42): a firm formed for a particular venture ends when the venture is completed, unless the partners agree otherwise.

(b) **Compulsory dissolution** (Section 41): the business has become unlawful, so the firm ends by law.

(c) **Dissolution by notice** (Section 43): in a partnership at will any partner may end the firm by written notice; it is dissolved from the date stated.

questions.stem_md: Explain any four modes by which a partnership firm may be dissolved.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each mode named and correctly explained, up to four.

answer.model_answer_md:
Any four of the following, each explained:

1. **By agreement (Section 40):** the firm is dissolved with the consent of all the partners, or in accordance with a contract between them.
2. **Compulsory dissolution (Section 41):** the firm ends by operation of law, whatever the partners wish, for example when its business becomes unlawful.
3. **On the happening of certain contingencies (Section 42):** unless the partners agree otherwise, the firm is dissolved on events such as the expiry of its fixed term, the completion of the venture for which it was formed, or the death of a partner.
4. **By notice (Section 43):** in a partnership at will, any partner may dissolve the firm by giving written notice to all the others.
5. **By the court (Section 44):** on a partner’s suit, on grounds such as unsound mind or permanent incapacity of a partner, misconduct, persistent breach of the agreement, transfer of a partner’s whole interest, a business that can run only at a loss, or any just and equitable ground.

questions.stem_md:
For each situation, state whether it is a dissolution of the partnership only or a dissolution of the firm, and name the mode where the firm is dissolved:

(a) Ruby retires from an imagined bakery in Kolkata; Sohan and Tina continue the business.
(b) The three partners of an imagined travel firm in Leh all agree to close it after a poor season.
(c) In an imagined transport firm in Ranchi, Ujjal keeps breaking the partnership agreement; Varun sues, and the court orders the firm to be wound up.
(d) An imagined firm in Bhuj was formed only to build one community hall, and the hall has been handed over.
questions.solution_md: First ask whether the business goes on; if it stops, find what caused it to stop.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Dissolution of the partnership only.** The firm is reconstituted: Sohan and Tina carry on the same business, so its books continue.

(b) **Dissolution of the firm, by agreement** (Section 40): all the partners consent to close the business.

(c) **Dissolution of the firm, by the court** (Section 44): persistent breach of the agreement is a ground on which the court may dissolve the firm on a partner’s suit.

(d) **Dissolution of the firm on the happening of a contingency** (Section 42): the venture for which it was formed is complete.

questions.stem_md: Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, the assets of a dissolved firm, including any sums contributed by partners to make up deficiencies, are first used to pay

options.text_md: loans given to the firm by partners
the partners’ capitals
any surplus to the partners in their profit-sharing ratio
the debts of the firm to third parties

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the debts of the firm to third parties. Outsiders come first; then partners’ advances (loans) rateably; then partners’ capitals rateably; and any residue is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.stem_md: Besides her capital, Esha has lent money to her firm. When the firm is dissolved, her loan is repaid

options.text_md: before the outside liabilities
after the outside liabilities but before any partner’s capital
after all the partners’ capitals
through her capital account along with her capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** after the outside liabilities but before any partner’s capital. Section 48 puts a partner’s advances after third-party debts and ahead of capital. The loan is settled directly from the bank: Esha’s Loan A/c Dr, To Bank A/c.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On dissolution, a partner’s loan to the firm is paid before the capitals of the partners are returned.

**Reason (R):** Section 48 ranks advances made by partners, as distinguished from capital, ahead of amounts due to them on account of capital.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R states the very rule of the Act that produces A.

questions.stem_md: Under Section 48, after paying the debts of the firm to third parties, the firm’s assets are used to repay partners’ ___ before returning their capitals.
questions.solution_md: Partners’ loans (advances) come next, before capital.

questions.stem_md: Explain the order in which the accounts of a firm are settled on its dissolution under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, in the absence of any agreement among the partners.
questions.solution_md: Rule (a) is about bearing losses; rule (b) is about the order of payments out of the assets.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Losses:** losses, including deficiencies of capital, are met first out of profits, next out of capital and, lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.

**(b) Application of assets** (including sums contributed by partners to make up deficiencies), in this order:
1. Debts of the firm to **third parties** (outside liabilities).
2. **Advances (loans)** made by each partner, rateably.
3. Amounts due to each partner on account of **capital**, rateably.
4. The **residue**, if any, divided among the partners in their **profit-sharing ratio**.

marking_scheme.step: Outside debts first, then partners’ loans
Capitals, then the residue in the profit-sharing ratio

questions.stem_md: Prakash, Qureshi and Ruchi share the profits of an imagined printing unit in Kanpur in the ratio 2:2:1. The firm is dissolved. After every asset has been sold and the realisation expenses paid, the firm has ₹3,05,000 at the bank. It owes creditors ₹1,20,000 and a bank loan of ₹50,000; Ruchi has also lent the firm ₹25,000. The capitals stand at Prakash ₹80,000, Qureshi ₹60,000 and Ruchi ₹30,000, and there are no reserves. Find the loss to be borne by the partners and show how the bank balance is paid out under Section 48.
questions.solution_md: The loss comes out of capital in the profit-sharing ratio; the bank balance is then used in the Section 48 order and is exactly used up.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Loss:** total claims = 1,20,000 + 50,000 + 25,000 + 1,70,000 = 3,65,000; cash available 3,05,000; shortfall = **60,000**, borne 2:2:1: Prakash 24,000, Qureshi 24,000, Ruchi 12,000.

| Order (Section 48) | Paid to | ₹ |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| 1. Outside liabilities | Creditors | 1,20,000 |
| 1. Outside liabilities | Bank loan | 50,000 |
| 2. Partner’s loan | Ruchi | 25,000 |
| 3. Capitals (after the loss) | Prakash 80,000 − 24,000 | 56,000 |
| 3. Capitals (after the loss) | Qureshi 60,000 − 24,000 | 36,000 |
| 3. Capitals (after the loss) | Ruchi 30,000 − 12,000 | 18,000 |
| **Total** | | **3,05,000** |

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **not** transferred to the Realisation Account when a firm is dissolved?

options.text_md: A partner’s loan to the firm
Bills payable
Provision for doubtful debts
Machinery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A partner’s loan to the firm. A partner’s loan is paid directly from the bank after outside liabilities. Machinery goes to the debit side; bills payable and the provision go to the credit side.

questions.stem_md: On dissolution, the Provision for Doubtful Debts appearing in the balance sheet is

options.text_md: debited to the Realisation Account
credited to the Realisation Account, the debtors being debited at their gross amount
credited to the partners’ capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
ignored, because debtors are transferred at their net amount

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** credited to the Realisation Account, the debtors being debited at their gross amount. Debtors go to the debit side at their full book amount and the provision against them goes to the credit side, so the net effect equals the net book value.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Provision for Doubtful Debts is credited to the Realisation Account on the dissolution of a firm.

**Reason (R):** Debtors are transferred to the Realisation Account at their net value after deducting the provision.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: debtors are transferred at their gross figure, and that is precisely why the provision has to be credited separately.

questions.stem_md: True or false? On dissolution, the bank balance of the firm is transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account along with the other assets.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Cash and bank are not realised: they are already money. They stay in the Cash or Bank Account, which records every receipt and payment and finally closes at nil.

questions.stem_md: Realisation Account is a ___ account, prepared to find the profit or loss on the sale of assets and the payment of liabilities.
questions.solution_md: It is a nominal account: it records gains and losses.

questions.stem_md: A General Reserve appearing in the balance sheet at the time of dissolution is

options.text_md: credited to the Realisation Account
debited to the Realisation Account
credited to the partners’ capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
credited to the partners’ capital accounts in their capital ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** credited to the partners’ capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio. A reserve is undistributed profit, so it belongs to the partners in the ratio in which they share profits; it never passes through realisation.

questions.stem_md: A debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account shown on the assets side of a firm’s balance sheet at the time of dissolution is

options.text_md: debited to the Realisation Account
credited to the partners’ capital accounts
transferred to the Bank Account
debited to the partners’ capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debited to the partners’ capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio. An accumulated loss is a fictitious asset that cannot be sold; it is written off against the partners’ capitals in their profit-sharing ratio.

questions.stem_md: Kunal and Lekha share profits 2:1 in an imagined two-wheeler workshop in Solapur, which they dissolve. Their balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹18,000, a debit balance of ₹6,000 in the Profit and Loss Account, an Advertisement Suspense (deferred advertisement expenditure) of ₹3,000 and a loan of ₹12,000 from Lekha. Pass the journal entries for these items, assuming the loan is repaid in full.
questions.solution_md: Reserves are credited and fictitious assets debited to capitals in the profit-sharing ratio; the partner’s loan is paid straight from the bank.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| General Reserve A/c Dr | 18,000 |   |
| To Kunal's Capital A/c |   | 12,000 |
| To Lekha's Capital A/c |   | 6,000 |
| *(Being general reserve distributed in the ratio 2:1)* |   |   |
| Kunal's Capital A/c Dr | 6,000 |   |
| Lekha's Capital A/c Dr | 3,000 |   |
| To Profit and Loss A/c |   | 6,000 |
| To Advertisement Suspense A/c |   | 3,000 |
| *(Being accumulated loss and deferred advertisement expenditure written off in the ratio 2:1)* |   |   |
| Lekha's Loan A/c Dr | 12,000 |   |
| To Bank A/c |   | 12,000 |
| *(Being Lekha's loan repaid)* |   |   |

None of these items passes through the Realisation Account.

marking_scheme.step: Loss and advertisement suspense written off

questions.stem_md: On dissolution, Kiran, a partner, takes over the firm’s car at an agreed value. The entry is

options.text_md: Realisation A/c Dr, To Kiran’s Capital A/c
Car A/c Dr, To Kiran’s Capital A/c
Kiran’s Capital A/c Dr, To Car A/c
Kiran’s Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Kiran’s Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c. The car is already on the debit of Realisation, so its value is now credited there; Kiran receives the car instead of money, so his capital is debited.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh, a partner, agrees to pay off the firm’s bills payable himself. The entry on dissolution is

options.text_md: Ramesh’s Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c
Bills Payable A/c Dr, To Ramesh’s Capital A/c
Realisation A/c Dr, To Ramesh’s Capital A/c
Realisation A/c Dr, To Bank A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Realisation A/c Dr, To Ramesh’s Capital A/c. Bills payable are already on the credit of Realisation; discharging them is a debit to Realisation, and Ramesh, who pays, is credited.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a partner takes over an asset of the firm on dissolution, the agreed value is credited to his capital account.

**Reason (R):** Taking over an asset reduces the amount finally payable to that partner.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: his capital account is debited, not credited. R is true, and it is the reason the debit is correct.

questions.stem_md: An old printer, fully written off and not shown in the books, is taken over by Sapna, a partner, at ₹2,500 when the firm is dissolved. The entry is

options.text_md: Realisation A/c Dr ₹2,500, To Sapna's Capital A/c ₹2,500
Sapna's Capital A/c Dr ₹2,500, To Realisation A/c ₹2,500
Printer A/c Dr ₹2,500, To Sapna's Capital A/c ₹2,500
No entry, because the printer is not in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Sapna's Capital A/c Dr ₹2,500, To Realisation A/c ₹2,500. An unrecorded asset taken over by a partner is a gain on realisation: credit Realisation and debit the partner’s capital with the agreed value.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An unrecorded liability paid by the firm at the time of dissolution is debited to the Realisation Account.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Paying it is an extra cost of closing the firm, so Realisation is debited and Bank credited.

questions.stem_md: A creditor of an imagined firm accepts a machine in full settlement of his claim. The machine and the creditor have both been transferred to the Realisation Account already. The entry is

options.text_md: no entry is passed
Creditors A/c Dr, To Machinery A/c
Realisation A/c Dr, To Machinery A/c
Creditors A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** no entry is passed. Both items are already in Realisation, and no cash moves, so nothing more needs recording; the difference between them is reflected in the realisation result automatically.

questions.stem_md: Yusuf, a partner, pays the realisation expenses out of his own pocket on behalf of the firm, and the firm is to bear them. The entry is

options.text_md: Yusuf’s Capital A/c Dr, To Realisation A/c
Realisation A/c Dr, To Yusuf’s Capital A/c
Realisation A/c Dr, To Bank A/c
no entry is needed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Realisation A/c Dr, To Yusuf’s Capital A/c. The expense belongs to the firm, so Realisation is debited; the firm now owes Yusuf, so his capital is credited.

questions.stem_md: Bindu, a partner, is to receive ₹6,000 for carrying out the dissolution of an imagined firm and is to bear all realisation expenses. The actual expenses of ₹4,500 are paid by the firm. The amount debited to the Realisation Account for the dissolution work is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹6,000. Only the agreed remuneration of 6,000 is the firm’s cost (Realisation Dr, To Bindu’s Capital). The 4,500 is Bindu’s own burden: Bindu’s Capital Dr, To Bank.

questions.stem_md: After every adjustment on dissolution, Arvind's capital account shows a debit balance of ₹7,000. The entry to settle it is

options.text_md: Bank A/c Dr ₹7,000, To Arvind's Capital A/c ₹7,000
Arvind's Capital A/c Dr ₹7,000, To Bank A/c ₹7,000
Realisation A/c Dr ₹7,000, To Arvind's Capital A/c ₹7,000
Arvind's Capital A/c Dr ₹7,000, To Realisation A/c ₹7,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Bank A/c Dr ₹7,000, To Arvind's Capital A/c ₹7,000. A debit balance means Arvind owes the firm; he brings in cash, so Bank is debited and his capital account is credited, which closes it.

An imagined cement agency in Sambalpur is dissolved; its creditors of ₹60,000 have been transferred to the Realisation Account. They are settled as follows:

(c) The remaining creditors are paid in cash at a discount of 2%.

questions.solution_md: Only the cash that leaves the firm is recorded; the asset handed over needs no entry.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **No entry.** The stock and the creditor are both already in the Realisation Account and no cash is paid.

(b) and (c):

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Realisation A/c Dr | 6,000 |   |
| To Bank A/c |   | 6,000 |
| *(Being balance paid to creditors who accepted machinery)* |   |   |
| Realisation A/c Dr | 14,700 |   |
| To Bank A/c |   | 14,700 |
| *(Being remaining creditors paid at a discount of 2%)* |   |   |

Workings: (b) 30,000 − 24,000 = 6,000; (c) remaining creditors 15,000 less 2% = 14,700.

questions.stem_md: Farhan, a partner in an imagined travel firm in Vijayawada, is appointed to complete the dissolution. He is to get a remuneration of ₹7,000 and to bear all realisation expenses himself. The expenses come to ₹5,200, which the firm pays on his behalf. Pass the journal entries and state the net effect on Farhan's capital account.
questions.solution_md: The remuneration is the firm’s cost; the expenses are the partner’s own, even when the firm pays them.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Realisation A/c Dr | 7,000 |   |
| To Farhan's Capital A/c |   | 7,000 |
| *(Being remuneration allowed to Farhan for carrying out the dissolution)* |   |   |
| Farhan's Capital A/c Dr | 5,200 |   |
| To Bank A/c |   | 5,200 |
| *(Being realisation expenses, to be borne by Farhan, paid by the firm)* |   |   |

Net effect: Farhan's capital rises by 7,000 − 5,200 = **1,800**. The Realisation Account bears only the agreed 7,000.

| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Bank A/c Dr | 7,500 |   |
| To Realisation A/c |   | 7,500 |

| Realisation A/c Dr | 2,400 |   |
| To Bank A/c |   | 2,400 |

| Jagdish's Capital A/c Dr | 1,500 |   |
| To Realisation A/c |   | 1,500 |
| *(Being unrecorded typewriter taken over by Jagdish)* |   |   |

Unrecorded assets bring a gain (credit Realisation); unrecorded liabilities bring a loss (debit Realisation).
